analysis.one_liner: Adds a capped home-care benefit to Medicare for help with daily living.
analysis.headline: The Medicare at Home Act was introduced with one cosponsor and referred to two House committees, where it has sat without action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new Medicare benefit paying home care workers to help older adults and disabled people with everyday tasks like bathing, dressing, eating, and medication reminders — up to 20 hours a week. Medicare today pays for short-term home health care but not long-term personal care at home, so families pay out of pocket (often more than $60,000 a year), spend down their savings into Medicaid, or go without. The bill finances the new benefit through Medicare's monthly Part B premiums rather than a new tax.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who need help with at least two daily living activities — roughly the more than 10 million beneficiaries who need such help — plus their unpaid family caregivers, who currently fill the gap. Home care workers also gain from a required reasonable wage floor in the payment system.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and disabled people needing daily care

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Medicare home care benefit covering help with activities of daily living (bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, eating) and instrumental activities (meals, medication reminders, light housekeeping), up to 20 hours per week [S2].

Eligibility requires certification that the person needs help with at least two activities of daily living or two instrumental activities, and excludes people already receiving duplicating long-term care through Medicaid [S2].
The bill's findings note home care paid out of pocket costs more than $60,000 annually, and that unpaid family caregivers provide over $1 trillion in unpaid care to the economy [S2].
Payment rules must reflect a reasonable wage floor for home care workers, and the bill's findings cite polling that 93 percent of adults believe Medicare should cover home care [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries, through higher monthly Part B premiums adjusted to the benefit's actuarial cost (about a quarter of Part B costs are also paid from general federal revenue under the standard subsidy schedule), plus taxpayers through that same subsidy. Home care agencies must meet new enrollment and worker-qualification standards.

drawbacks.text: The benefit is financed by raising Part B premiums on beneficiaries, so older people pay for the new coverage through their own monthly bills rather than through general revenue [S2].
The benefit is capped at 20 hours per week, which may not cover the full needs of people with heavy care requirements, leaving some families still paying out of pocket or relying on Medicaid [S2].

Implementation is slow: regulations are due within a year and the benefit does not start until more than two years after enactment, and the bill directs HHS to write worker-qualification and agency-enrollment standards that could be difficult or costly to meet [S2].

Because eligibility is limited to people not already receiving duplicating Medicaid home care, the benefit could sit alongside, rather than simplify, the existing patchwork of long-term care programs [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families facing $60,000-a-year home care bills or burning through savings to qualify for Medicaid, a 20-hour-a-week Medicare benefit would be substantial relief, even though the premium increase that funds it falls on the same beneficiaries. The cap and the exclusion of people already on Medicaid limit who is helped, and the financing choice makes premiums rather than broad taxes bear the cost — a real tradeoff, but one weighted toward helping people stay out of nursing homes and out of poverty.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2026 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, which have taken no further action on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 3, 2026, by Rep. Debbie Dingell and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee [S1][S4].
It has one cosponsor, a Democrat [S3].
No hearings, markups, votes, or further floor action appear in the action history [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has lost anything and nothing has changed; the outcome hinges on whether the committees act.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No change yet; status quo holds

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare at Home Act and referred it to two House committees.

sides.party_line_note: With only the sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, there is no roll-call or voting record from which to read a partisan split.

industries.note: The bill makes Medicare-covered home care flow through enrolled agencies and individual home care workers, creating a large new paid customer base for the industry while subjecting it to new wage-floor, qualification, and enrollment rules. For beneficiaries, this means care arrives through the existing home care industry rather than a government-run service.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and institutional long-term care
industries.note: A home care benefit reduces pressure to place people in institutions, which the bill's findings identify as a costlier outcome of the current system. Institutional providers would face slower demand growth.

The bill excludes people already receiving duplicating Medicaid home care, so states do not lose their existing caseload, but the new Medicare benefit could relieve some future spend-down into Medicaid, easing state costs over time.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to two committees late in a two-year Congress with a single cosponsor rarely receive a markup or floor vote; unless the committees schedule action in the remaining months, this bill will die in committee at the end of the session on January 3, 2027.
